deep.reconstruction:
Page 124 continues Euler's table of primes of the form a^2+1 for even a from 256 to 1146. The table runs on from p.123 (a up to 250) and finishes on p.125 (a up to 1494).

How the table was made: on the preceding pages Euler built a table of the divisors of a^2+1 for a up to 1500. Any prime divisor p of a^2+1 is 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4). The roots of a^2 ≡ -1 (mod p) recur with period p, so the divisors can be sieved along arithmetic progressions a ≡ ±r_p (mod p). The values of a not hit by any odd p ≤ sqrt(a^2+1) give primes, which are listed here.

The purpose of the paper (E283, 'De numeris primis valde magnis') is to exhibit many explicitly certified large primes, beyond 100000 and even beyond 10^6, at a time when factor tables reached only about 10^5. The form a^2+1 is used because its divisors are so restricted.

This page has three columns of 28 entries each. The first two columns run a = 256 to 816. The third runs a = 826 to 1146 and includes the first values above 10^6 (a = 1004, 1008017 onward).
errors: Arithmetic: all 84 entries on this page check, i.e. each listed number equals a^2+1 exactly.

Primality: the cumulative count of listed a ≤ 1000 is 42 (p.123) + 70 (this page, through a = 986) = 112. This agrees with the modern count of n ≤ 1000 with n^2+1 prime (19 for n ≤ 100, 112 for n ≤ 1000), so the table appears complete and correct through a = 1000. I sieved 67601 and 1008017 by hand partially and found no small factors. Entries with a > 1000 were not individually verified.

Not on this page, but nearby: the text on p.125 says there are 112 primes > 100000. Counting the tables as transcribed (from a = 326 on) gives 19 + 28 + 28 + 35 = 110. Euler's count of 49 primes above a million does check. Coincidentally, 112 is exactly the number of listed primes with a ≤ 1000 counted from a = 1.
Also on p.125, not this page: the entry 1434 → 2056351 should read 2056357, since 1434^2 = 2056356.

ideas.what: Sieve-generated table of primes n^2+1, using the restriction p ≡ 1 mod 4 and the periodicity of the roots of x^2 ≡ -1 mod p
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic-polynomial sieve; primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's 4th problem; OEIS A002496/A005574)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E283) for the first extensive table. The later tables are by Cunningham and others, then computer tables.
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 9 (1764); Opera Omnia I.3

ideas.what: Explicit primes exceeding 10^6 certified via the special form a^2+1
ideas.modern_name: Primality certification via special forms (records of known large primes)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a pure numerical table that is well known in the history of prime tables, and it is correct through a = 1000 when checked against the modern count of 112. The only flaws found are minor slips on the next page: a misprint and a probable miscount. Nothing here is uncredited or unexplored.
transcription_corrections: Header of the first column reads 'Numeri pri-mi aa+1' (the image has 'Nameri pri mi', a print or scan artefact). Otherwise the machine transcription of all 84 entries matches the image.
